name: Wernicke encephalopathy

matching.reasoningTemplate: Confusion, ataxia and eye signs in an alcohol-dependent or malnourished patient is Wernicke until proven otherwise.

redFlags: Reversible — treat empirically with thiamine, do not delay

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.2348-2350 (Ch.318 Nervous System Disorders in Critical Care); p.2607 (Ch.344 Vitamin/Trace Mineral Deficiency); p.235-236 (Ch. Disorders of the Eye); p.3526 (Ch.464 Alcohol/neurology of amnesia); p.3719 (Ch. Alcohol Use Disorders)
clinicalPearls: The classic triad (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, global confusion) is present in only about one-third of acute cases, so a complete triad should not be required to make the diagnosis.
Most patients are profoundly disoriented, apathetic/indifferent, and inattentive rather than agitated; agitated delirium, when present, is usually from coexisting alcohol withdrawal.

Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke is not confined to alcohol use; non-alcoholic risk groups include hyperemesis, starvation/malnutrition, renal dialysis, cancer, HIV/AIDS, gastric/bariatric surgery, and chronic diuretic therapy (increased urinary thiamine loss).
Certain drugs (e.g., metformin, verapamil) can inhibit intestinal thiamine transporters (ThTR-2) and add to deficiency risk.

Ocular signs include horizontal nystagmus on lateral gaze, bilateral lateral rectus (abducens) palsy, conjugate gaze palsies, and rarely ptosis; pupils are usually spared but may become miotic in advanced disease.
Gait ataxia is multifactorial, arising from a combination of peripheral polyneuropathy, cerebellar involvement, and vestibular paresis.
Treat on clinical suspicion as a medical emergency: it is common, preventable, and reversible if thiamine is given early.
Korsakoff amnestic state may only become apparent as the acute confusion recedes, characterized by recent-memory/learning impairment, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing.
The amnestic deficit correlates with lesions of the dorsomedial (dorsal medial) thalamic nuclei.
harrison.pathophysiology: Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Deficiency causes a diffuse fall in cerebral glucose utilization and mitochondrial damage; impaired alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase leads to glutamate accumulation, which together with the energy deficit may produce excitotoxic neuronal injury. Lesions are periventricular, surrounding the third ventricle, aqueduct, and fourth ventricle, with predilection for midline structures (dorsomedial thalamus, mammillary bodies, midline cerebellum, periaqueductal gray, and trochlear/abducens nuclei). Acute cases may show petechial hemorrhages; chronic cases show mammillary body atrophy.
additionalDifferentials: Supranuclear gaze disorder mimicking combined abducens and oculomotor nerve palsy (Wernicke can itself cause this pattern)
Other metabolic encephalopathies (hepatic, hypercarbic, hyper-/hyponatremic, hyper-/hypoglycemic)
Marchiafava-Bignami disease (corpus callosum degeneration in chronic alcoholism)
infectionMimics: Encephalitis (including herpes simplex encephalitis as a cause of an amnestic state)
Whipple's disease (cause of supranuclear gaze palsy)
nonInfectiousMimics: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis (e.g., AMPAR, LGI1 antibodies) causing amnesia
Thalamic, medial temporal, or posterior corpus callosum tumor causing amnesia
Anterior/posterior cerebral artery territory infarction causing amnesia
Stroke (infarct/hemorrhage), multiple sclerosis, vasculitis, or tumor causing supranuclear gaze palsy
additionalInvestigations: MRI may show changes including abnormal enhancement of the mammillary bodies (coronal T1 postcontrast), typical of acute Wernicke
Erythrocyte transketolase activity assay measured before and after adding thiamine pyrophosphate; >25% stimulation (activity coefficient >=1.25) is abnormal
Serum/blood thiamine or its phosphorylated esters by high-performance liquid chromatography
Serum magnesium (required cofactor for thiamine activation)
redFlags: Untreated disease can progress to stupor, coma, and death
Giving glucose (parenteral dextrose) before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke in a previously unaffected at-risk patient or rapidly worsen an early form
New amnestic state emerging as confusion clears signals evolution to Korsakoff syndrome
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on early thiamine administration. Ocular palsies improve within hours of thiamine; horizontal nystagmus may persist. Ataxia improves more slowly than ocular signs, and roughly half of patients recover incompletely, left with a slow, wide-based, shuffling gait and inability to tandem walk. Apathy, drowsiness, and confusion resolve gradually. Korsakoff psychosis is frequently persistent, with permanent gaps in memory, confabulation, and disordered temporal sequencing; prolonged untreated deficiency can cause an irreversible profound amnestic syndrome or death. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is underdiagnosed despite a typical history and picture.
pitfalls: Waiting for the full classic triad before treating, when only about one-third of patients show all three features.
Attributing the quiet, indifferent, inattentive confusional state to depression, sedation, or simple intoxication and missing the diagnosis.
Assuming Wernicke occurs only in alcoholics and overlooking it in hyperemesis, malnutrition, dialysis, bariatric surgery, cancer, or HIV patients.
Administering glucose-containing fluids before thiamine in an at-risk patient, which can trigger or worsen Wernicke.
Thiamine deficiency being overlooked in the setting of head injury (and possibly contributing to motor vehicle accidents).
